newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand has a recent history of mass murders.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand has a recent history of mass murders.

text.p: Despite the image of tranquility it likes to project, New Zealand has a recent history of mass slayings. Saturday's shotgun rampage added six dead and five wounded to the list of victims.
Up until 1990s the only twentieth century mass murder was conducted by Stanley Graham in 1941. He shot six people including five policemen before he was shot by police after a massive manhunt.
But the list in the 1990s is extensive:

* On November 13, 1990 David Gray, 33, slaughtered 13 people during 24 hours of terror in the tiny Otago seaside settlement of Aramoana in the southern South Island. He used a semi-automatic assault rifle. Two of the victims died in a fire. Police finally shot Gray dead. He had seven guns and four had been used in the shootings. Gray was a loner with an intense interest in weapons.

* On May 20, 1992, grandfather and farmer Brian Schlaepfer, 64, shot or stabbed six members of his family at their farm near Pukekohe, south of Auckland. Schlaepfer shot himself immediately with his shotgun after the killings. The coroner's hearing concluded Schlaepfer was suffering from depression.

* On June 26, 1992 Raymond Ratima bludgeoned or stabbed to death seven people including his three sons and other family members. Ratima was sentenced to mandatory life imprisonment. A psychiatric report said he was jealous, anti-social and believed he could control the lives of his wife and children.

* On June 20, 1994 David Bain shot five members of his family with a .22 rifle including his parents two sisters and brother. Bain, a university student, maintains his innocence, saying his father committed the murders and committed suicide. The father had had an incestuous relationship with one of the daughters.

* On February 8, 1997, a 24-year old man went on a shotgun shooting spree in the central North Island hamlet of Raurimu. Six people were killed and five seriously wounded. Few details have been officially released but residents say the victims were mostly family members and the suspect had a history of psychiatric problems. Police arrested him stark naked.
The latest shooting spree has spurred fresh calls by anti-gun lobbists to tighten up firearms laws.

"Why must we always wait for yet another gun massacre before we tighten our firearms laws," said gun policy researcher Philip Alpers. "Comprehensive new gun laws in Australia, Britain and Canada have left New Zealand out on a limb."

He said Britain acted quickly after the Dunblane massacre where 16 children and their teacher were shot dead last year as did Australia following the Port Arthur spree in which 35 people were gunned down.
Alpers said New Zealand had a gun for every household and 11 times as many guns per capita as in Britain.
If the suspect of the Raurimu massacre is found to have had psychiatric problems the heat may also go on the mental health service as well.
New Zealand has recently opened up its mental institutions and released many people with mental problems into the community.
Health authorities say they released people into the community because people get well better there, but critics claim it has been done to economise and support is lacking.
The new system has come under scrutiny after a spate of crimes involving people with psychiatric problems and claims that those involved have received little or no support from the health system.
